style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare Greek transliterations in amp with Strong's carried in notes; em-dashes used sparingly; transliterations ASCII-normalized relative to the lexicon's spellings.
chapterNote: The tongue, and the two wisdoms. James begins at the teacher's desk -- not many of you should take it, for the mouth-trade is judged by a stricter standard -- and then widens to every mouth in the room. Three small things that steer great masses: the bit in the horse's mouth, the tiny rudder under the storm-driven ship, the spark ahead of the forest fire. The tongue is all three, a little member boasting great things: a fire, a world of unrighteousness among our members, staining the whole body, setting the wheel of existence ablaze, and drawing its own flame up from Gehenna. Mankind has tamed every order of creature, but no man tames the tongue -- restless evil, full of death-dealing poison -- and its deepest scandal is the double stream: blessing God and cursing men made in His likeness from the same opening, which no spring in nature would tolerate. The chapter then traces speech to its source: bitter envy and selfish ambition are a 'wisdom' from below, earthly, unspiritual, demonic, breeding disorder; the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruit, undivided and unfeigned -- and the harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

1.text: My brothers, not many of you should become teachers, since you know that we who teach will receive the stricter judgment.
1.amp: My brethren [adelphos], be not many [polus] masters [didaskalos -- teachers], knowing [eido] that we shall receive [lambano] the greater [meizon] condemnation ['judgment', krima, the KJV margin].
1.notes: didaskalos (G1320) was the seat of honor the assembly coveted; James, himself a teacher, says 'we' -- he stands under the same meizon krima (G2917). Words multiplied professionally multiply liability (cf. Matthew 12:36-37).

2.text: For in many ways we all stumble. The one who never stumbles in what he says is a man come to maturity, able to keep the whole body under the bridle as well.
2.amp: For in many things [polus] we offend [ptaio -- stumble] all [hapas]. If any man offend not in word [logos], the same is a perfect [teleios -- mature, complete] man [aner], and able [dunatos] also to bridle [chalinagogeo] the whole [holos] body [soma].
2.notes: ptaio (G4417), the stumbling-word of 2:10, now confessed universally -- hapas (G537), all of us, teacher included. The tongue is the last outpost conquered: the man who rules it is teleios (G5046), and chalinagogeo (G5468), the bridle-verb of 1:26, extends his rein over the whole soma.

3.text: Look how we put bits into horses' mouths to make them obey us, and we turn their whole body.
3.amp: Behold [idou], we put [ballo] bits [chalinos] in the horses' [hippos] mouths [stoma], that they may obey [peitho] us; and we turn about [metago] their whole [holos] body [soma].
3.notes: The chalinos (G5469), a few ounces of iron in a half-ton hippos (G2462): control of the stoma is control of the animal. The analogy runs both directions -- master the mouth and the man follows; leave it unbitted and it carries him where it will.

4.text: Look at the ships too: huge as they are, and driven by fierce winds, they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the impulse of the pilot decides.
4.amp: Behold [idou] also the ships [ploion], which though they be so great [telikoutos], and are driven [elauno] of fierce [skleros -- hard, violent] winds [anemos], yet are they turned about [metago] with a very small [elachistos] helm [pedalion -- rudder], whithersoever the governor [euthuno -- the one steering straight] wills [boulomai].
4.notes: Second exhibit, scaled up: the pedalion (G4079), elachistos (G1646), smallest of the ship's parts, overrules skleros anemos (G4642, G417), the hard winds themselves. The steering question is never the size of the vessel or the weather but whose hand is on the helm.

5.text: So also the tongue is a little member, and it boasts of great things. Look how great a forest a little fire sets alight!
5.amp: Even so the tongue [glossa] is a little [mikros] member [melos], and boasts great things [megalaucheo]. Behold [idou], how great [helikos] a matter ['wood', hule -- a forest, the KJV margin] a little [oligos] fire [pur] kindles [anapto]!
5.notes: megalaucheo (G3166), to boast greatly -- and the boast is not empty, which is the horror of it. The third exhibit turns dark: bit and rudder steer, but pur (G4442) only consumes, and the hule (G5208), the standing forest, is a lifetime of relationships, reputations, and churches.

6.text: And the tongue is a fire, the very world of unrighteousness. The tongue is set among our members as the one that stains the whole body, sets the wheel of existence burning, and is itself set burning by Gehenna.
6.amp: And the tongue [glossa] is a fire [pur], a world [kosmos] of iniquity [adikia]: so is the tongue among our members [melos], that it defiles [spiloo -- stains, spots] the whole [holos] body [soma], and sets on fire [phlogizo] the course ['wheel', trochos, the KJV margin] of nature [genesis], and it is set on fire [phlogizo] of hell [geenna].
6.notes: A kosmos of adikia (G2889, G93): the whole world's evil, miniaturized and installed behind the teeth. spiloo (G4695) undoes the aspilos, the unspottedness, of 1:27; the trochos genesis (G5164, G1078) is the whole rolling wheel of existence from birth onward. The arson investigation closes at the source: geenna (G1067) supplies the flame.

7.text: For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, is being tamed and has been tamed by mankind,
7.amp: For every kind ['nature', phusis, the KJV margin] of beasts [therion], and of birds [peteinon], and of serpents [herpeton], and of things in the sea [enalios], is tamed [damazo -- subdued], and has been tamed of mankind [anthropinos phusis -- the nature of man]:
7.notes: The four zoological orders echo the dominion mandate of Genesis 1:26 and 9:2: land, air, ground-creepers, sea. damazo (G1150), twice -- the taming is both ongoing and accomplished. Man has broken lions and charmed herpeton (G2062); one wild thing remains.

8.text: but the tongue no man can tame: a restless evil, full of death-bearing poison.
8.amp: But the tongue [glossa] can no man [anthropos] tame [damazo]; it is an unruly [akataschetos -- unrestrainable, restless] evil [kakos], full [mestos] of deadly [thanatephoros -- death-bearing] poison [ios].
8.notes: akataschetos (G183) is kin to the akatastatos instability of the double-souled man in 1:8: the untamed tongue never holds still. ios (G2447) is venom -- the serpent's weapon (cf. Psalm 140:3), carried not in a fang but under the palate. No man tames it; the chapter leaves room for God to.

9.text: With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men, who are made in the likeness of God.
9.amp: Therewith bless we [eulogeo -- speak well of] God [theos], even the Father [pater]; and therewith curse we [kataraomai] men [anthropos], which are made [ginomai] after [kata] the similitude [homoiosis -- likeness] of God.
9.notes: eulogeo (G2127) and the curse (G2672) from one instrument: Sunday's doxology and Monday's contempt. The argument against cursing men is Genesis 1:26 -- the homoiosis (G3669) of God stands in the man being cursed, so the curse ricochets upward toward the Blessed One Himself.

10.text: Out of the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.
10.amp: Out of the same [autos] mouth [stoma] proceeds [exerchomai] blessing [eulogia] and cursing [katara]. My brethren [adelphos], these things ought [chre] not so to be [ginomai].
10.notes: The one stoma (G4750), two streams. chre (G5534), 'it ought not' -- the only occurrence of this word in the New Testament, as if James reached for a term he never otherwise needed: this is against nature itself, as the next verse proves from the landscape.

11.text: Does a spring pour out sweet water and bitter from the same opening?
11.amp: Does a fountain [pege -- a spring] send forth [bruo -- gush] at the same place ['hole', ope, the KJV margin] sweet [glukus] water and bitter [pikros]?
11.notes: bruo (G1032) is to gush and teem: springs pour what they hold, without editing. glukus (G1099) and pikros (G4089) cannot share one ope because a spring has only one source -- the question every double mouth must answer about its heart.

12.text: Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives, or a grapevine figs? Neither can a salt spring yield sweet water.
12.amp: Can the fig tree [suke], my brethren [adelphos], bear [poieo] olive berries [elaia]? either a vine [ampelos], figs [sukon]? so can no fountain [pege] both yield salt [halukos -- brackish] water [hudor] and fresh [glukus].
12.notes: The orchard test his Brother taught: a tree is known by its fruit (cf. Matthew 7:16-20). suke, elaia, ampelos (G4808, G1636, G288) -- each yields after its kind, and a halukos (G252) spring has settled the question of what it is. Speech is fruit; the root decides.

13.text: Who among you is wise and understanding? Let him show it by his good manner of life, his works done in wisdom's own meekness.
13.amp: Who is a wise man [sophos] and endued with knowledge [epistemon -- understanding, skilled] among you? let him show [deiknumi] out of a good [kalos] conversation [anastrophe -- manner of life, conduct] his works [ergon] with meekness [prautes] of wisdom [sophia].
13.notes: The demonstration-demand of 2:18 applied to wisdom: deiknumi (G1166), show it. The exhibit is anastrophe (G391), the whole turned life, and the signature of true sophia (G4678) is prautes (G4240) -- strength under God's rein, the same meekness that received the word in 1:21.

14.text: But if you harbor bitter envy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast of it and lie against the truth.
14.amp: But if you have bitter [pikros] envying [zelos -- jealousy, rivalry-zeal] and strife [eritheia -- selfish ambition, faction] in your hearts [kardia], glory [katakauchaomai -- boast] not, and lie [pseudomai] not against [kata] the truth [aletheia].
14.notes: pikros (G4089), the bitter water of verse 11, located: in the kardia. zelos (G2205) is zeal soured into rivalry, and eritheia (G2052) the office-seeker's ambition, party spirit. Calling that drive 'wisdom' is the lie against aletheia (G225) -- gifted, driven, and wrong.

15.text: That is not the wisdom that comes down from above; it is earthly, unspiritual, demonic.
15.amp: This wisdom [sophia] descends [katerchomai] not from above [anothen], but is earthly [epigeios], sensual ['natural', psuchikos, the KJV margin -- of the unspiritual soul], devilish [daimoniodes -- demon-like].
15.notes: Three descending steps: epigeios (G1919), horizon-bound; psuchikos (G5591), running on the natural soul without the Spirit; daimoniodes (G1141), bearing the demons' own family likeness -- for the demons of 2:19 also have their cleverness. anothen (G509) is the watershed: wisdom is known by its source.

16.text: For where envy and selfish ambition are, there is disorder and every worthless practice.
16.amp: For where envying [zelos] and strife [eritheia] is, there is confusion [akatastasia -- disorder, tumult] and every [pas] evil [phaulos -- worthless, vile] work [pragma].
16.notes: akatastasia (G181) completes the word-family of the letter: unstable man (1:8), untamable tongue (3:8), and now the unquiet church. Where zelos and eritheia set the agenda, disorder is not a risk but a law, and every phaulos pragma (G5337, G4229) finds the door unlocked.

17.text: But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, easy to be entreated, full of mercy and good fruits, undivided in judgment, and without hypocrisy.
17.amp: But the wisdom [sophia] that is from above [anothen] is first [proton] pure [hagnos], then [epeita] peaceable [eirenikos], gentle [epieikes -- forbearing, reasonable], and easy to be intreated [eupeithes -- readily persuaded to good], full [mestos] of mercy [eleos] and good [agathos] fruits [karpos], without partiality [adiakritos -- undivided, impartial], and without hypocrisy [anupokritos -- unfeigned].
17.notes: proton hagnos (G4412, G53): purity leads, before even peace -- heaven's wisdom will not buy calm at truth's expense, yet everything after is warmth: eirenikos (G1516), epieikes (G1933), eupeithes (G2138). adiakritos (G87) finally heals the letter's disease-word diakrino -- wisdom from above does not waver or play favorites, and anupokritos (G505) wears no mask.

18.text: And the harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by the ones who are making peace.
18.amp: And the fruit [karpos] of righteousness [dikaiosune] is sown [speiro] in peace [eirene] of them that make [poieo] peace [eirene].
18.notes: The farmer's paradox: a karpos that must be speiro (G4687), sown, and the seed is eirene itself. dikaiosune (G1343) -- the very thing man's anger could not produce in 1:20 -- grows in soil the peacemakers keep; his Brother's beatitude stands behind every word (cf. Matthew 5:9).
